cues.text: OK, Jim. You wanted to see me about your textile design project.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: That’s right. I’ve been looking at how a range of natural dyes can be used to colour fabrics like cotton and wool.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: Why did you choose that topic?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Well, I got a lot of useful ideas from the museum, you know, at that exhibition of textiles. But I’ve always been interested in anything to do with colour. Years ago, I went to a carpet shop with my parents when we were on holiday in Turkey, and I remember all the amazing colours.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: They might not all have been natural dyes.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Maybe not, but for the project I decided to follow it up. And I found a great book about a botanic garden in California that specialises in plants used for dyes.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: OK. So, in your project, you had to include a practical investigation.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Yeah. At first I couldn’t decide on my variables. I was going to just look at one type of fibre for example, like cotton …
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: … and see how different types of dyes affected it?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Yes. Then I decided to include others as well, so I looked at cotton and wool and nylon.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: With just one type of dye
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Various types, including some that weren’t natural, for comparison.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: OK.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: So, I did the experiments last week. I used some ready-made natural dyes. I found a website which supplied them, they came in just a few days, but I also made some of my own.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: That must have taken quite a bit of time.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Yes, I’d thought it’d just be a matter of a teaspoon or so of dye, and actually that wasn’t the case at all. Like I was using one vegetable, beetroot, for a red dye, and I had to chop up a whole pile of it. So it all took longer than I’d expected.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: One possibility is to use food colourings.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: I did use one. That was a yellow dye, an artificial one.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: Tartrazine?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Yeah. I used it on cotton first. It came out a great colour, but when I rinsed the material, the colour just washed away. I’d been going to try it out on nylon, but I abandoned that idea.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: Were you worried about health issues?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: I’d thought if it’s a legal food colouring, it must be safe.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: Well, it can occasionally cause allergic reactions, I believe.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: So what natural dyes did you look at?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Well, one was turmeric. The colour’s great, it’s a really strong yellow. It’s generally used in dishes like curry.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: It’s meant to be quite good for your health when eaten, but you might find it’s not permanent when it’s used as a dye – a few washes, and it’s gone.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Right. I used beetroot as a dye for wool. When I chop up beetroot to eat I always end up with bright red hands, but the wool ended up just a sort of watery cream shade. Disappointing.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: There’s a natural dye called Tyrian purple. Have you heard of that?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Yes. It comes from a shellfish, and it was worn in ancient times but only by important people as it was so rare. I didn’t use it.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: It fell out of use centuries ago, though one researcher managed to get hold of some recently. But that shade of purple can be produced by chemical dyes nowadays. Did you use any black dyes?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Logwood. That was quite complicated. I had to prepare the fabric so the dye would take.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: I hope you were careful to wear gloves.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Yes. I know the danger with that dye.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: Good. It can be extremely dangerous if it’s ingested. Now, presumably you had a look at an insect-based dye? Like cochineal, for example?
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: Yes. I didn’t actually make that, I didn’t have time to start crushing up insects to get the red colour and anyway they’re not available here, but I managed to get the dye quite easily from a website. But it cost a fortune. I can see why it’s generally just used in cooking, and in small quantities.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: Yes, it’s very effective, but that’s precisely why it’s not used as a dye.
cues.speaker: TUTOR

cues.text: I also read about using metal oxide. Apparently you can allow iron to rust while it’s in contact with the fabric, and that colours it.
cues.speaker: JIM

cues.text: Yes, that works well for dying cotton. But you have to be careful as the metal can actually affect the fabric and so you can’t expect to get a lot of wear out of fabrics treated in this way. And the colours are quite subtle, not everyone likes them. Anyway, it looks as if you’ve done a lot of work …
cues.speaker: TUTOR
